content.overview: Section 46(1) provides that a certificate, issued under the common seal, if any, of the company or signed by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary, wherever the company has appointed a Company Secretary, specifying the shares held by any person, shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the person to such shares. Section 46(2) provides that a duplicate certificate of shares may be issued if such certificate is proved to have been lost or destroyed, or has been defaced, mutilated or torn and is surrendered to the company. Section 46(3) provides that, notwithstanding anything contained in the articles of a company, the manner of issue of a certificate of shares or the duplicate thereof, the form of such certificate, the particulars to be entered in the register of members and other matters shall be such as may be prescribed. Section 46(4) provides that where a share is held in depository form, the record of the depository is the prima facie evidence of the interest of the beneficial owner. Section 46(5) provides that if a company with intent to defraud issues a duplicate certificate of shares, the company shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than five times the face value of the shares involved in the issue of the duplicate certificate but which may extend to ten times the face value of such shares or rupees ten crore, whichever is higher, and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable for action under section 447.
content.glance: Certificate (seal or signed by two directors / director+CS) is prima facie evidence of title; duplicates if lost/destroyed or defaced/mutilated/torn and surrendered; prescribed manner/form; demat record is prima facie evidence; fraudulent duplicate — fine 5×–10× face value or ₹10 crore (whichever higher) + s. 447 for officers.
content.study: A certificate issued under the common seal, if any, or signed by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary (where appointed), specifying the shares held, is prima facie evidence of title (s. 46(1)). A duplicate may be issued if the original is proved lost or destroyed, or is defaced, mutilated or torn and surrendered (s. 46(2)). Manner, form and register particulars are as prescribed, notwithstanding the articles (s. 46(3)). For demat shares, the depository record is prima facie evidence of the beneficial owner’s interest (s. 46(4)). Fraudulent issue of a duplicate attracts fine of not less than five times the face value, extending to ten times the face value or ₹10 crore (whichever higher), and officers are liable under s. 447 (s. 46(5)). Current-law framing: identify certificate or demat record; apply prima facie rule; address duplicates and fraud penalty.

sections.heading: Prima facie evidence (s. 46(1))
sections.body: Certificate issued under common seal (if any) or signed by two directors or by a director and the Company Secretary is prima facie evidence of title to the shares specified.

sections.heading: Duplicate certificates (s. 46(2))
sections.body: May be issued if original is proved lost or destroyed, or is defaced, mutilated or torn and is surrendered to the company.

sections.heading: Prescribed manner (s. 46(3))
sections.body: Manner of issue, form of certificate, register particulars and other matters shall be as prescribed, notwithstanding the articles.

sections.heading: Demat record (s. 46(4))
sections.body: Where a share is held in depository form, the depository’s record is the prima facie evidence of the interest of the beneficial owner.

sections.heading: Fraudulent duplicate (s. 46(5))
sections.body: If a company with intent to defraud issues a duplicate certificate, fine not less than five times the face value, up to ten times the face value or ₹10 crore (whichever higher); officers in default liable under section 447.

examples.title: Valid certificate
examples.body: A certificate signed by two directors specifying the member’s shares is prima facie evidence of that member’s title under s. 46(1).

examples.title: Lost certificate
examples.body: Member proves loss of original and seeks duplicate under s. 46(2).

examples.title: Fraudulent duplicate
examples.body: Company issues a duplicate with intent to defraud. Section 46(5) penalty applies (5×–10× face value or ₹10 crore, whichever higher) and officers face s. 447.

hypotheticals.question: Is a share certificate conclusive evidence of title?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 46 makes it prima facie evidence only.

hypotheticals.question: What is the evidence of title for demat shares?
hypotheticals.analysis: The record of the depository is the prima facie evidence under s. 46(4).

distinctions.title: Certificate of shares (s. 46) vs numbering of shares (s. 45)

misconceptions.trap: A share certificate is conclusive and cannot be challenged.
misconceptions.correction: Section 46 makes it only prima facie evidence of title.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 46 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify certificate or demat record. II. Apply prima facie evidence rule. III. Address duplicates/formalities/fraud if relevant. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Certificate authenticity; prima facie title; any challenge; duplicate conditions if claimed; fraud penalty if alleged; precise relief.

examTips: Mention demat record, duplicates and s. 46(5) fraud penalty.
